## Related Work

**LM Output Diversity and Mode Collapse.**
The tendency of language models to produce repetitive or degenerate text has been recognized since early work on neural text generation. Holtzman et al. [1] identified that maximization-based decoding leads to repetitive, incoherent outputs and proposed nucleus sampling to preserve diversity. Subsequent work has introduced decoding-level interventions such as min-p sampling [2], which dynamically adjusts the truncation threshold based on model confidence to improve output diversity at higher temperatures. Beyond decoding, several benchmarks now systematically evaluate LM generation diversity. NoveltyBench [3] evaluates the ability of LMs to produce multiple distinct, high-quality outputs across subjective, creative, and knowledge-based prompts, revealing that larger models within the same family often exhibit less diversity than their smaller counterparts. Guo et al. [4] proposed a framework for benchmarking linguistic diversity across lexical, syntactic, and semantic dimensions, finding that state-of-the-art LLMs significantly underperform human text in syntactic and semantic variation, particularly after preference tuning. Yun et al. [5] identified diversity collapse induced by structured prompt templates, showing that format tokens act as behavioral anchors that constrain the output space even under high-temperature sampling. At a broader level, Briesch et al. [6] demonstrated that training LLMs in a self-consuming loop on their own outputs progressively reduces generation diversity. While these works establish important foundations, existing benchmarks predominantly target stylized or narrow tasks and do not capture the full spectrum of real-world open-ended user queries. Moreover, prior studies have largely focused on intra-model repetition; the phenomenon of inter-model homogeneity—where distinct models independently converge on similar outputs—remains underexplored. This motivates the target paper's systematic study of both intra- and inter-model mode collapse across a broad set of models on real-world open-ended prompts.

**Real-World Open-Ended Query Resources.**
Understanding the types of open-ended queries users pose to LMs requires datasets grounded in authentic interactions. WildChat [7] provides a corpus of one million real-world user-ChatGPT conversations, capturing diverse languages, interaction patterns, and use cases far richer than curated instruction-tuning datasets. Wang et al. [8] developed a taxonomy of user intents in LLM interactions based on real-world logs, identifying categories such as creative generation, learning, and decision support. However, neither resource provides a systematic taxonomy of open-ended query types specifically designed to elicit diverse responses, nor do they couple query categorization with model diversity evaluation. This motivates the target paper's construction of INFINITY-CHAT, which combines a comprehensive open-ended query taxonomy with large-scale diversity analysis and dense human annotations.

**Automated Evaluation and Pluralistic Alignment for Open-Ended Tasks.**
Evaluating open-ended LM outputs requires handling subjective and often divergent human preferences. Zhang et al. [9] analyzed sources of annotator disagreement in preference datasets, finding that over 30% of disagreements stem from genuine preference divergence rather than annotation noise, and showed that standard Bradley-Terry reward models fail to distinguish between unanimous and divided preferences. To address this, pluralistic alignment frameworks have been proposed. Chen et al. [10] introduced PAL, which models heterogeneous human preferences as a mixture of latent prototypes, enabling reward functions that generalize to unseen users. Halpern et al. [12] proposed pairwise-calibrated reward ensembles that directly match the distribution of annotator preferences without requiring annotator identity labels. On the evaluation side, the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm [11] has emerged as a scalable alternative to human evaluation for open-ended tasks, but its reliability under high annotator disagreement and for responses of comparable quality remains poorly understood. These lines of work highlight the need for dense human annotations that capture distributional preferences, as well as reward models and judges that are calibrated to the full spectrum of human judgments on open-ended queries—gaps that the target paper addresses through its large-scale annotation study.

\section{Related Work}
The diversity collapse problem of LMs. Diversity collapse, characterized by the inability of LMs to generate diverse outputs, presents a significant challenge to pluralistic alignment research [96, 78, 23, 93, 53, 91]. Prior studies identify some key factors contributing to diversity collapse, including training on synthetic data [33, 86, 93, 79], LM alignment [58, 41, 43], and insufficient diversity in training data [15]. Potential consequences of diversity collapse include reduced creativity, loss of minority perspectives, spread of bias, and overall decline in model utility and trustworthiness [5, 38, 21]. In response, a range of mitigation strategies are proposed, such as training corpora diversification [87, 68, 88, 34], training algorithm modifications [95, 54], alternative decoding [85, 62] and prompting [94, 11] strategies.

Measuring the creativity and divergent thinking of language models. Recent efforts to measure the creativity and divergent thinking of LMs often adapt established psychometric tests. For example, [16] utilizes a divergent association task (DAT) by asking models to generate semantically distant or unrelated words [63]. Similarly, tasks such as the Alternate Uses Test (AUT) [69], the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) [1, 13], Human Evaluation, and LLM-as-a-judge [46] are employed to assess dimensions like fluency, originality, complexity, and effective semantic diversity [80] of LM responses. Despite these demonstrated capabilities, LLM-generated creative content tends towards homogeneity, even when individual outputs achieve high creativity scores [90]. To address these evaluation complexities, some benchmarks, such as [72, 56, 66, 95], focus on specific creative abilities like scientific idea and code generation. Other works propose new metrics [61]. While LMs show promise in creative tasks, comprehensively evaluating their creativity remains an active and challenging research area [44]. We conduct a large-scale systematic study of real-world open-ended user queries and provide a comprehensive taxonomy, query dataset, and dense human annotations to improve evaluation and model training for reducing mode collapse in language models.

Disagreement and pluralistic alignment of language models. Advances in AI value alignment research have substantially improved LM utility and safety, through enhanced training processes [75, 64, 70], and the use of both synthetic data [30] and human datasets [8, 29]. Yet, a significant challenge remains: the potential for monolithic value representation [73, 74]. In contrast, the emerging focus on pluralistic alignment emphasizes the need for AI to serve the varied demands of a wide population [81, 2]. This shift is driving innovation in methods [19, 62, 49, 14, 26, 83], benchmarks [12], and data collection strategies [42, 76] to support this vision of diversity. Additionally, approaches leveraging multiple LMs interacting through system messages are also being explored to boost variety [84, 17, 59]. \section{Related Work}
The diversity collapse problem of LMs. Diversity collapse, characterized by the inability of LMs to generate diverse outputs, presents a significant challenge to pluralistic alignment research [96, 78, 23, 93, 53, 91]. Prior studies identify some key factors contributing to diversity collapse, including training on synthetic data [33, 86, 93, 79], LM alignment [58, 41, 43], and insufficient diversity in training data [15]. Potential consequences of diversity collapse include reduced creativity, loss of minority perspectives, spread of bias, and overall decline in model utility and trustworthiness [5, 38, 21]. In response, a range of mitigation strategies are proposed, such as training corpora diversification [87, 68, 88, 34], training algorithm modifications [95, 54], alternative decoding [85, 62] and prompting [94, 11] strategies.

Measuring the creativity and divergent thinking of language models. Recent efforts to measure the creativity and divergent thinking of LMs often adapt established psychometric tests. For example, [16] utilizes a divergent association task (DAT) by asking models to generate semantically distant or unrelated words [63]. Similarly, tasks such as the Alternate Uses Test (AUT) [69], the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) [1, 13], Human Evaluation, and LLM-as-a-judge [46] are employed to assess dimensions like fluency, originality, complexity, and effective semantic diversity [80] of LM responses. Despite these demonstrated capabilities, LLM-generated creative content tends towards homogeneity, even when individual outputs achieve high creativity scores [90]. To address these evaluation complexities, some benchmarks, such as [72, 56, 66, 95], focus on specific creative abilities like scientific idea and code generation. Other works propose new metrics [61]. While LMs show promise in creative tasks, comprehensively evaluating their creativity remains an active and challenging research area [44]. We conduct a large-scale systematic study of real-world open-ended user queries and provide a comprehensive taxonomy, query dataset, and dense human annotations to improve evaluation and model training for reducing mode collapse in language models.

Disagreement and pluralistic alignment of language models. Advances in AI value alignment research have substantially improved LM utility and safety, through enhanced training processes [75, 64, 70], and the use of both synthetic data [30] and human datasets [8, 29]. Yet, a significant challenge remains: the potential for monolithic value representation [73, 74]. In contrast, the emerging focus on pluralistic alignment emphasizes the need for AI to serve the varied demands of a wide population [81, 2]. This shift is driving innovation in methods [19, 62, 49, 14, 26, 83], benchmarks [12], and data collection strategies [42, 76] to support this vision of diversity. Additionally, approaches leveraging multiple LMs interacting through system messages are also being explored to boost variety [84, 17, 59]. Parallel efforts are dedicated to quantifying and improving the cultural diversity exhibited by LLMs [71, 77, 18, 60, 52]. Yet, a common characteristic of many existing pluralistic alignment work is its reliance on predefined diversity dimensions, like demographics [48, 57], personality style [51, 35, 98, 65], and cultural background [92, 22, 4]. To enable models that genuinely cater to individuality without relying on stereotypes, individual-level alignment is needed [36, 98].

s2_metadata.title: Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

tldr.text: [research paper] The paper presents a comprehensive study of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for training language models to be helpful and harmless. It introduces an iterated online RLHF training process where preference models and policies are updated weekly with fresh human feedback, leading to sustained improvements in both helpfulness and harmlessness. A key finding is a roughly linear relationship between the RL reward and the square root of the KL divergence between policy and initialization, indicating a predictable trade-off in policy divergence. The results show that RLHF does not degrade performance on most NLP tasks—especially for larger models—and can be effectively combined with specialized skill training (e.g., code generation) without compromising alignment or capability.

topics.label: LM Output Diversity and Mode Collapse
topics.summary: This section reviews prior work on language model output diversity and mode collapse, including decoding interventions (nucleus sampling, min-p sampling), benchmarks for diversity evaluation (NoveltyBench, linguistic diversity frameworks), and studies on diversity collapse from prompts and self-consuming training. It notes a gap in real-world open-ended query evaluation and inter-model homogeneity.

topics.label: Real-World Open-Ended Query Resources
topics.summary: This section discusses datasets and taxonomies for open-ended user queries, specifically WildChat and Wang et al.'s intent taxonomy. It highlights the absence of a query taxonomy coupled with diversity evaluation, motivating the construction of INFINITY-CHAT.

topics.label: Automated Evaluation and Pluralistic Alignment for Open-Ended Tasks
topics.summary: This section covers challenges in evaluating open-ended LM outputs, including annotator disagreement and pluralistic alignment methods (PAL, pairwise-calibrated rewards). It also discusses the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm and its limitations, motivating the need for dense human annotations and calibrated models.

claims.text: Holtzman et al. [1] identified that maximization-based decoding leads to repetitive, incoherent outputs and proposed nucleus sampling to preserve diversity.
Min-p sampling [2] dynamically adjusts truncation threshold based on model confidence to improve output diversity at higher temperatures.

NoveltyBench [3] evaluates the ability of LMs to produce multiple distinct, high-quality outputs across subjective, creative, and knowledge-based prompts, revealing that larger models within the same family often exhibit less diversity.

Guo et al. [4] proposed a framework for benchmarking linguistic diversity across lexical, syntactic, and semantic dimensions, finding that state-of-the-art LLMs underperform human text in syntactic and semantic variation, particularly after preference tuning.

Wang et al. [8] developed a taxonomy of user intents in LLM interactions based on real-world logs, identifying categories such as creative generation, learning, and decision support.

[9] analyzed sources of annotator disagreement in preference datasets, finding that over 30% of disagreements stem from genuine preference divergence rather than annotation noise, and showed that standard Bradley-Terry reward models fail to distinguish between unanimous and divided preferences.
